content: In organic chemistry, the term butyl refers to a four-carbon alkyl substituent with the chemical formula C4H9. This group is derived from one of the two isomers of butane, a four-carbon alkane. Each of the two isomers of butane can give rise to two distinct isomers of the butyl group. For n-butane, the connection can occur at either a terminal carbon atom or an internal carbon atom. This results in two isomers: The n-butyl group, with the structure CH3CH2CH2CH2–, which is systematically named butyl. The sec-butyl group, with the structure CH3CH2(CH3)CH–, which is systematically named 1-methylpropyl. The second isomer of butane, isobutane, can also form two distinct butyl groups depending on whether the connection occurs at a terminal methyl group or an internal carbon atom. These are: The isobutyl group, with the structure (CH3)2CHCH2–, which is systematically named 2-methylpropyl. The tert-butyl group, with the structure (CH3)3C–, which is systematically named 1,1-dimethylethyl. Nomenclature According to IUPAC nomenclature, the names isobutyl, sec-butyl, and tert-butyl are considered retained trivial names. Butyl is the largest alkyl substituent for which trivial names are commonly used for all its isomers. The prefixes iso, sec, and tert indicate the number of carbons attached to the primary carbon (the carbon directly bonded to the rest of the molecule). Specifically: Iso indicates one carbon attached. Secindicates two carbons attached. Tertindicates three carbons attached. Etymology The name butyl is historically derived from butyric acid, a four-carbon carboxylic acid found in rancid butter. The term butyric itself originates from the Latin word butyrum, meaning butter. As the number of carbons in alkyl chains increases, butyl is the last group to be named historically rather than systematically using Greek numerical prefixes. tert-Butyl Effect The tert-butyl group is notably bulky and is often used in chemistry to provide kinetic stabilization, especially in conjunction with other bulky groups like the related trimethylsilyl group. The influence of the tert-butyl group on the rate of a chemical reaction is referred to as the tert-butyl effect. This effect is exemplified in the Diels-Alder reaction, where the presence of a tert-butyl substituent accelerates the reaction rate by a factor of 240 compared to when hydrogen is the substituent.
